messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: prob propto 1/sigma
parts:
From Andrew:

> ... is there a way we can include that prior p(sigma) proportional to 1/sigma more transparently, instead of increment_log_prob? Or maybe increment_log_prob is the clearest approach.


I assume

increment_log_prob(log(1/sigma));

is not what you meant :-)

It's not a proper density is it? Should we add improper densities?
We could also add an improper:

y ~ flat();

If so, you can make a feature request on GitHub, and preferably
again let us know about priority? Or I can do it if you think we
should.

You can almost get there with a Pareto with very small
shape and lower bound, as in:

sigma ~ pareto(1e-30, 1e-30);

which will make sigma proportional to (1/y)^(1 + 1e-30), and the
1 + 1e-30 will underflow to 1. But it also requires that pesky
lower bound.

- Bob

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] prob propto 1/sigma
parts:
If sigma is constrained, i.e. sigma<lower=0>, then the Jacobian essentially
gives the 1/sigma prior. Remember, 1/sigma implies uniform for log(sigma).

Remember that by default we just don’t add anything to the log posterior except for the Jacobian.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] prob propto 1/sigma
parts:
The parameters are all uniform by default on their
constrained values.

So if you declare:

real<lower=0> sigma;

then sigma is uniform on (0,inf).

What happens under the hood is that there is an unconstrained
parameter sigma_raw with support on (-inf,inf), and then
sigma is defined by the inverse-log transform:

sigma <- exp(sigma_raw);

and the total log probability is incremented by the log Jacobian,
here log(abs(exp'(sigma_raw))) = sigma_raw, so that the effect is

lp__ <- lp__ + sigma_raw;

The unconstrained representantations and Jacobians are all
detailed in a chapter near the end of the manual.

So when Andrew takes sigma propto 1/sigma, the effect is:

lp__ <- lp__ + log(1/sigma);

which reduces to

lp__ <- lp__ - sigma;

so it cancels the Jacobian and leaves the transform of
sigma uniform, i.e., log(sigma) propto constant.

And before anyone asks, let me say that Stan isn't smart
enough to avoid adding sigma and subtracting sigma --- it
just does both operations and calculates gradients with respect
to both and it all cancels arithmetically, not symbolically.

- Bob
